newsitem.title: USA: Father of supercomputer Seymour Cray dies.
newsitem.headline: Father of supercomputer Seymour Cray dies.

text.p: Seymour Cray, known as the father of the supercomputer, died on Saturday nearly two weeks after suffering serious injuries in a car accident, a hospital spokeswoman said.
"Seymour Cray died at 2:53 am (4:53 EDT/0853 GMT). The cause of death was complications from massive head injuries," said Kate Brewster, spokeswoman at Penrose Community Hospital.
Cray had been in the hospital since Sept. 22 when his vehicle was hit by another car on Interstate-25 in Colorado Springs. He turned 71 on Sept. 28.

Cray is credited with developing the first fully transistorized supercomputer in 1958, and after he formed his own company bearing his name in the 1970s, his name became synonymous with cutting-edge technology.
Cray's place in the history books is assured, said Norris Parker Smith, editor-at-large of HPC Wire, an on-line publication that tracks the high-performance computer industry.
"He introduced innovations and carried them into very influential products," Smith said.

In 1957, with Bill Norris, Cray started Control Corp., and then founded Cray Research in Minnesota in 1972. Many of Cray's supercomputers -- large machines that can process large amounts of data at great speeds -- were used by the U.S. government, including the military.
Supercomputers have been used to design nuclear weapons, build geographic models for detecting oil deposits, and in cryptography -- or code making.
Cray left Cray Research to establish Cray Computer in Colorado Springs, Colorado in 1989. The two companies were not related and Cray Research was sold to Silicon Graphics Inc. earlier this year.

Whether there was room for another supercomputing company was doubtful and the Colorado firm -- which never sold a single machine -- filed for bankruptcy in 1995 after it failed to attract some $20 million needed from investors.

The advent of the personal computer that delivered high power right to the desk of scientists and engineers and slimmer defence budgets meant less demand for supercomputers, whose pricetag can run as high as $30 million.
"He stayed with the technology that he had espoused after other alternatives came along that were more successful," Smith said, adding that was both his flaw and his strength.

Nevertheless, Cray was undaunted. The man who once said he wanted to "die with my boots on," announced in August he was back in business with SRC Computers Inc., although details were sketchy on the company's brief.

The later years belie Cray's contribution. The years of work for the Department of Defence were the heady days. Cray told Science magazine in 1978 that he believed the ability to test bombs on a computer "seems to me to be the vehicle that led to the Test Ban Treaty, and as long as we can keep it on a computer no one will get hurt."
Fiercely independent, Cray was a loner and shy. In 1992 as a shareholder meeting was breaking up he was overheard telling investors "I really love what I do."
